ch01.anchor: an unlucky date
ch01.note: The Chinese says plainly that the day was unlucky in Western eyes (在西方人眼里). Thirteen carries no such charge in Chinese, where the ominous number is four, 四 sì, being a near-homophone of 死 sǐ, to die. The author opens by borrowing a foreign superstition to cast a shadow, a small piece of exoticism that reads as portentous in Chinese and merely flat in English.

ch01.anchor: flying the Blue Sky, White Sun, and Wholly Red Earth
ch01.note: 青天白日满地红, the full descriptive name of the Nationalist flag: a white twelve-rayed sun on a blue canton, on a red field. The canton was designed by Lu Haodong in 1895; Sun Yat-sen added the red field in 1906. The Guangzhou government adopted it in May 1921, but it did not become the official national flag of the Republic until December 1928 — over a year after this scene. In October 1927 it was still the flag of one faction among several, and the Five-Colored Flag remained the Republic's nominal standard. So a warship flying it on the Yangtze is making a claim, not stating a fact: this vessel belongs to Chiang's Nanjing regime. Chinese names the flag by describing it, which English cannot do without sounding like a heraldic label.

ch01.anchor: She had steamed down from Wuhu
ch01.note: Wuhu, a treaty port on the Yangtze in southern Anhui and Chen Diaoyuan's provincial base. The run downriver to Pukou is roughly 100 km.

ch01.anchor: Chen Diaoyuan, Superintendent of Military Affairs for Anhui Province
ch01.note: Chen Diaoyuan (陈调元, born 1886 in Xinxian, Hebei) was a Beiyang officer who served a succession of masters — the Zhili clique, then the Fengtian army after surrendering Xuzhou without a fight, then Sun Chuanfang — before secretly opening negotiations with the Northern Expedition and going over to the Nationalists in early 1927 with more than twenty thousand men. Chiang made him commander of the new 37th Army and handed him Anhui. The book's contempt for him as a professional turncoat is the standard verdict, though sources vary on the details of his career. 军务督办, Superintendent of Military Affairs, is a Beiyang-era provincial military governorship held separately from civil office; the author stacks Chen's titles deliberately, to show a man accumulating everything at once.

ch01.anchor: Son of a bitch. So the Chen bastard really came.
ch01.note: 他妈的 and 王八蛋 in the original. The first is the standard all-purpose Chinese obscenity, literally "his mother's," with the object of the verb left unsaid. The second is literally "turtle's egg," an old and genuinely cutting insult implying the man's mother was unfaithful and his paternity unknown. English has no equivalent that keeps the specific slur about parentage without sounding archaic, so "bastard" carries it at the cost of the animal.

ch01.anchor: Under a tree near the wharf
ch01.note: The tree is uncertain. The scan degrades exactly here and the character recognition returns 黄栏机 and 黄柳树 on successive passes, neither of which is a word. The most likely reading is 黄桷树 (also written 黄葛树), Ficus virens, a large fig common in southwest China — which is what produced "banyan" in an earlier draft of this translation. But that species is unusual in Nanjing, and 黄杨 (boxwood) and other 木-radical tree names are equally consistent with the damaged glyph. I have left the tree unnamed in the English rather than assert a species I cannot read. Anyone with access to a clean copy of the second edition could settle it in a moment.

ch01.anchor: a man got up as a seller of Jinling dates
ch01.note: 金陵, Jinling, is the classical literary name for Nanjing, still used for local products and in elevated prose. So the disguise is specifically that of a Nanjing street hawker, not a generic peddler.

ch01.anchor: every man with a Mauser in his fist
ch01.note: 盒子枪, literally "box gun": the Mauser C96 "broomhandle," so called in Chinese for the wooden holster that doubled as a shoulder stock. Also known as 驳壳枪 or 盒子炮. It was the defining sidearm of the Republican era, carried by warlord guards, gangsters and Communist commanders alike, and its appearance in a scene is a period marker as precise as a Thompson gun in an American one.

ch01.anchor: the head of the Hatchet Gang, Wang Yaqiao
ch01.note: 斧头帮. Most English writing renders this "Axe Gang," but 斧头 is a hand axe or hatchet, and the organisation took its name from the small axes that Anhui dockworkers carried for cutting cargo ropes — Wang is said to have had a hundred of them forged overnight during a labour dispute around 1921. I have used "Hatchet Gang" both because it is the more accurate object and because "Axe Gang" now drags in associations from Stephen Chow's Kung Fu Hustle that would badly mislead a reader here. The gang grew out of Anhui native-place and labour associations in Shanghai and became a political assassination outfit rather than a conventional criminal syndicate.

ch01.anchor: This was the Hefei notable they called the Ninth Master
ch01.note: 九爷, "Ninth Master." 爷 is a term of deference for a senior man in this world, closer to "boss" or "the old man" than to any English word for master. The nine comes from Wang's courtesy name 九光, Jiuguang, which he uses of himself later in this section. English cannot show that the honorific and the name are the same nine, so the connection that is obvious on the page in Chinese has to be pointed at here instead.

ch01.anchor: a pot of aged nü'erhong
ch01.note: 女儿红, "daughter's red," a Shaoxing yellow rice wine traditionally buried in the ground when a daughter is born and dug up for her wedding feast. It is the wine of celebrations and long patience. The author has Wang drinking it while he waits to kill a man, which is either a fine touch or an accident of stock vocabulary; the register of the detail is entirely lost if you simply call it rice wine.

ch01.anchor: commander of the 37th Army of the National Revolutionary Army and commander-in-chief of the Northern Route Army besides
ch01.note: The character recognition read 莱 here, which is meaningless; the scan clearly shows 兼, "concurrently holding," a bureaucratic term that does real work in this sentence by piling one command on top of another. The 37th Army was the formation created for Chen on his defection.

ch01.anchor: Bo Wenwei, commander of the 33rd Army
ch01.note: 柏文蔚 (1876–1947), an Anhui revolutionary of the older generation: Tongmenghui member, military governor of Anhui after the 1911 revolution, and a participant in the Second Revolution against Yuan Shikai. His real connection to Wang Yaqiao is documented — Bo was elected chairman of the Anhui Labour Union in Shanghai while Wang actually ran it — which is the factual seed the book grows into this teacher-and-disciple relationship. Note the arithmetic of the scene: the 33rd Army for the old revolutionary, the 37th for the man who changed sides last year.

ch01.anchor: He plays the tiger's jackal
ch01.note: 为虎作伥. A 伥 chāng is the ghost of a person eaten by a tiger, condemned to serve the beast by luring fresh victims into its path. The idiom therefore means far more than "accomplice": it carries the idea of a soul already devoured, doing the devourer's work, unable to stop. No English phrase reaches it. "Jackal" gets the servility and loses the horror.

ch01.anchor: It's the flesh and marrow of the people of Anhui
ch01.note: 民脂民膏, "the people's fat and the people's grease." A classical formula for wealth squeezed out of the governed, best known from the admonition carved on stone before magistrates' halls under the Song, warning officials that their salaries were paid in exactly this substance. To a Chinese reader the phrase arrives with the weight of a thousand years of official moralising behind it; in English it can only sound like vivid metaphor.

ch01.anchor: several warships were bearing toward him in an A formation
ch01.note: 呈A字形 — the original really does use the Latin letter A. Chinese more often describes such shapes with a character, as in 人字形 for a chevron. The Roman letter is a small modernism, and slightly incongruous in a 1927 scene.

ch01.anchor: aboard the *Dongzheng*
ch01.note: 东征号, the Eastern Expedition, named for the 1925 campaigns in Guangdong that made Chiang's military reputation.

ch01.anchor: greeted Chiang first with a student's formal bow
ch01.note: 执学生大礼, "performed the full ritual of a student." Chen is claiming the relation of disciple to teacher, the hierarchy that bound the Whampoa Military Academy officers to Chiang — despite having no Whampoa background whatever. That is precisely why it works. The gesture converts a defeated rival into a junior member of Chiang's own house, and Chiang, who valued that hierarchy above nearly everything, takes the offer.

ch01.anchor: British mortars and Krupp field guns
ch01.note: I flagged this in an earlier pass as the sort of colourful detail the genre invents, and I was wrong: independent accounts of Chen Diaoyuan's defection also report that he presented Chiang with a consignment of first-rate weapons to demonstrate his sincerity. The book's version is embroidered but not fabricated. Krupp guns were the standard German field artillery of the period and widely held by Chinese armies.

ch01.anchor: ranged in neat order on the deck
ch01.note: The Chinese reads 二门炮, literally "two guns" — 门 being the measure word for artillery pieces. That sits badly against the preceding sentence, which says the deck was loaded with artillery of every kind. Either the author means the two types just named, which is how I have translated it, or the figure is simply careless. I have checked the characters twice against the scan at magnification; the text does read 二.

ch01.anchor: I heard you were a Westernized officer
ch01.note: 洋军官. 洋 means foreign in the specific sense of Western, and carries a faint edge — 洋 things are modern, impressive and not quite ours. Chiang's compliment is therefore backhanded and double-edged: I had heard you were too foreign, and I find you know your manners after all. The sting and the flattery are the same sentence.

ch01.anchor: the governance of Anhui belongs to no one but you
ch01.note: 非君莫属, a set literary phrase of high courtesy meaning roughly "it could fall to no one but you, sir." Chiang shifts register upward at the exact moment he hands over a province.

ch01.anchor: became the piece Chiang Kai-shek planted on the Anhui board
ch01.note: 棋子, a playing piece in weiqi or Chinese chess. The metaphor is a commonplace of Chinese political writing and unremarkable in the original; "pawn" would be too contemptuous and too specifically Western, since weiqi has no ranked pieces. The reading of these characters is somewhat uncertain in the scan, but the sense is not in doubt.

ch01.anchor: Wang Yaqiao might have been Mount Tai
ch01.note: 安若泰山, "as settled as Mount Tai." Taishan, the eastern sacred peak in Shandong, is the standard Chinese figure for absolute immovability, the way a rock is in English but with the added weight of imperial pilgrimage and state ritual. It recurs constantly in fixed phrases.

ch01.anchor: what medicine his chief was selling from that gourd of his
ch01.note: 葫芦里卖的什么药, an everyday idiom for unreadable intentions. The image is an itinerant medicine seller whose wares are hidden inside an opaque dried gourd, so no one can tell what he is peddling until it is bought. I have kept it literal rather than flattening it to "what he was up to," because the gourd is the whole flavour of the line.

ch01.anchor: I, Wang Jiuguang, deal squarely with the world
ch01.note: 王九光. Wang naming himself in full mid-oath is a register marker with no English equivalent — it is the verbal equivalent of standing up. It also settles a question the translation had to resolve: 九光 is Wang Yaqiao's own courtesy name, so the speech earlier in this section beginning "Jiuguang, my friend" is Bo Wenwei addressing Wang, not Wang addressing a third party. An earlier draft of this translation left that ambiguous.

ch01.anchor: on his way to call on Chiang Kai-shek
ch01.note: The tactical reasoning is worth pausing on, because it is the book's thesis in miniature. Wang is not calling off the killing; he is relocating it, so that Chen's death reads as a message addressed to Chiang. This is assassination as political communication, which is what distinguished Wang Yaqiao from the Green Gang bosses he competed with. He would go on to attempt Chiang himself at Lushan in 1931 and to organise the killing that wounded Wang Jingwei in 1935.

ch01.anchor: that political hoodlum, Chiang the Baldhead
ch01.note: 蒋光头, "Chiang Bald-head," a standard derisive epithet of the period referring to Chiang's shaven scalp. It sounds cruder in Chinese than "the Baldhead" does in English, closer to a schoolyard name, and its constant use by his enemies was a small ongoing insult to a man extremely conscious of dignity.

ch01.anchor: the show they had been preparing since dawn had closed before the curtain ever rose
ch01.note: 一场好戏，还没开场就已经谢幕了 — literally "a fine opera that took its curtain call before the curtain ever went up." 开场 and 谢幕 are both theatre terms. Worth flagging because I nearly lost this line: the scan cut off mid-sentence at the foot of the page and an earlier draft closed the section with an invented sentence of my own. The author's ending is better than the one I made up, which is a useful lesson about where translation errors come from.

ch01.anchor: Wang Yaqiao had drained a bowl of blood-wine
ch01.note: 血酒. Wine mixed with blood, drunk to seal an oath of brotherhood or a vow. The gesture places Wang's promise to Bo Wenwei in the register of sworn kinship rather than mere agreement.

ch01.anchor: Zhang Wensheng, a former military governor of Anhui
ch01.note: 张文生, a Beiyang general who held Anhui in the early 1920s under the Zhili clique. The book's claim that Wang Yaqiao's agitation helped drive him from office is put in his own mouth here and I have not verified it independently. 寓公, the word behind "comfortable retirement," is a specific Republican type: an ex-official living privately, often in a treaty port or the capital, on the proceeds of office.

ch01.anchor: Once bitten by a snake, you shy at a well-rope for ten years
ch01.note: 一朝被蛇咬，十年怕井绳 — the coiled rope at a well's edge looks enough like a snake to make a bitten man flinch. One of the most common of all Chinese proverbs, and given here in its standard form; the scan is damaged at exactly this phrase and the number of years is not fully legible.

ch01.anchor: Who's eaten a leopard's gall
ch01.note: 吃了豹子胆, "eaten a leopard's gall": in traditional physiology the gall bladder is the seat of daring — 胆 appears in nearly every Chinese word for courage — so to have eaten a leopard's is to have swallowed courage beyond your station. English keeps the organ ("gall") but has lost the anatomy behind it.

ch01.anchor: betraying Wu Peifu and Cao Kun
ch01.note: Wu Peifu and Cao Kun were the leading figures of the Zhili clique, the Beiyang faction Chen Diaoyuan originally served. Cao Kun had bought the presidency of the Republic outright in 1923, one thousand silver dollars per parliamentary vote — worth knowing when the book's characters talk about corruption as though it began with Chen.

ch01.anchor: a pauper magnate second only to Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng
ch01.note: 穷大亨, "poor tycoon," a deliberate oxymoron: Wang commanded gang power on the scale of the great racketeers while holding, and distributing, comparatively little money. Huang Jinrong — simultaneously the top Chinese detective in the French Concession police and a crime boss — and Du Yuesheng, master of the opium trade and later Chiang's indispensable ally, were the two summits of the Green Gang. Contemporary accounts agree that these two genuinely preferred to avoid the Hatchet Gang rather than fight it, which for Shanghai in the 1920s is a remarkable fact.

ch01.anchor: the Shanghai militarist Sun Wancheng
ch01.note: The episode is broadly consistent with the record — Wang Yaqiao did raise a force at Hefei around the 1911 revolution and was driven out — but I cannot attest this commander's name in English-language scholarship, and the scan is rough here; the romanization is provisional.

ch01.anchor: Wang Yaqiao's Maicheng days
ch01.note: 走麦城, "walking to Maicheng." Maicheng is where Guan Yu — the greatest hero of the Three Kingdoms, later deified as the god of war — made his last retreat and was captured and executed. To "walk to Maicheng" is the proverbial figure for a great man's season of defeat. Zhang Wensheng is being literate and slightly mocking at once.

ch01.anchor: He attached himself to Jiang Kanghu
ch01.note: 江亢虎 (1883–1954), founder of the Chinese Socialist Party in 1911, the first party in China to carry the name. This detail is genuine history: Wang Yaqiao really did join the party and head its Anhui branch, and Yuan Shikai really did suppress it as he moved toward his imperial restoration. Jiang Kanghu's own road ended badly — he served in Wang Jingwei's collaborationist government during the Japanese occupation and died in a Communist prison.

ch01.anchor: Under Purple Mountain the autumn rain
ch01.note: 紫金山, Purple-Gold Mountain, the peak that overhangs Nanjing on the east. Its slopes hold the Ming founder's tomb and, from 1929, Sun Yat-sen's mausoleum — which gives the mountain's shadow over this chapter a certain irony the author may or may not intend, given whose testament Wang believes he is enforcing.

ch01.anchor: near the Gate of China
ch01.note: 中华门, the immense southern gate of the Nanjing city wall, the largest such gate-fortress in China; the surrounding wards were dense, poor, and easy to disappear into.

ch01.anchor: the old loach
ch01.note: 老泥鳅. The loach is a mudfish, impossible to hold: it slips through the fingers and buries itself in the bottom. Applied to a man it means a slippery survivor — and the sentence extends the same image, 沉沙卧底, "sunk into the sand to lie on the bottom." The metaphor is continuous in the Chinese in a way English can only gesture at.

ch01.anchor: Why hasn't he gone to the Confucius Temple
ch01.note: The Confucius Temple quarter (夫子庙) on the Qinhuai River was Nanjing's pleasure district — theatres, teahouses, sing-song houses. Wang's question is not about the sage; it means "why isn't he out among the singing girls?" The reply — that the women are brought to him by the carload — answers it in kind.

ch01.anchor: his Hatchet Gang lieutenant Kan Peilin
ch01.note: The scan is damaged at this name. The surname-glyph as scanned is not a surname at all; 阚 (Kan), a genuine and reasonably common Anhui surname of similar shape, is my best reading, and I have not found the man in outside sources. Treat the romanization as provisional.

ch01.anchor: ally with Russia, ally with the Communists, assist the peasants and workers
ch01.note: 联俄、联共、扶助农工, the "Three Great Policies" of Sun Yat-sen's last years, the basis of the first United Front with the Communist Party. Whether they represented Sun's true final position or a Soviet-brokered expedient became, after his death in March 1925, the central scriptural dispute of Chinese politics; Chiang's April 1927 purge of the Communists in Shanghai — six months before this scene — was its bloodiest answer. The author has Wang stake his whole vendetta on the orthodox-disciple reading.

ch01.anchor: his eye can't take a grain of sand
ch01.note: 眼里揉不进沙子, said of a man who cannot let the smallest offence pass. Bo's whole speech runs on set phrases — the next is 小巫见大巫, "the small shaman meeting the great one," rendered here as the small ghost calling on the great one — and the effect in Chinese is of an old man reaching for proverbs because plain words won't carry his alarm.

ch01.anchor: I'm a bare-stick proletarian
ch01.note: 光棍 — literally "bare stick" or "bare stalk" — means an unattached man: no wife, no property, no ties, and therefore nothing that can be held hostage. Wang's boast is precise: Chiang's forms of leverage need something to grip. The same word appeared earlier where Zhang Wensheng says Wang "stood up a made man" in Shanghai (立起了光棍儿), where it carries its other shading: an established tough, a man of the rivers-and-lakes world.

ch01.anchor: a chicken's gut for grievances
ch01.note: 小肚鸡肠, "small belly, chicken intestines": no room inside for anything to pass through, hence petty and unforgiving. The judgment of Chiang as a man who never forgot a slight is one point on which his admirers and his enemies broadly agreed.

ch01.anchor: the drunkard's interest is not in the wine
ch01.note: 醉翁之意不在酒 — from Ouyang Xiu's "Record of the Old Drunkard's Pavilion" (1046), where the writer says his pleasure is not really in the wine but in the mountains and streams. A thousand years of use have worn it into the standard way of saying "my stated purpose is not my real one." That a gang boss reaches for an eleventh-century essayist mid-conspiracy is entirely natural in Chinese and untranslatably strange in English.

ch01.anchor: killing the chicken for the monkey to see
ch01.note: 杀鸡给猴看: the trainer kills a chicken in front of the monkey, and the monkey — too valuable to harm directly — draws the conclusion. This is the chapter's thesis stated as barnyard proverb: Chen is the chicken; Chiang is the monkey.

ch01.anchor: the Jing Ke of our history
ch01.note: 荆轲, the most famous assassin in Chinese history, sent in 227 BC against the future First Emperor with a dagger rolled in a map. He failed and was cut down; the verse he sang at the river crossing — the wind sighs, the Yi water is cold; the hero once gone will not return — has stood ever since for the man who accepts death in the act of tyrannicide. Bo Wenwei's blessing is double-edged in a way English can't compress: Jing Ke is glorious, and Jing Ke did not come back. The section heading of the book's thirteenth chapter quotes the same verse, so the author is planting the figure early.

ch01.anchor: squatting here like frogs at the bottom of a well
ch01.note: The well-frog (井底之蛙), from Zhuangzi: the frog at the bottom of a well believes its circle of sky is the whole of it. Standard shorthand for complacent ignorance; Wang applies it to his own men, which is how the author lets him be furious and self-critical in one breath.

ch01.anchor: Zhang Qiubai — Commissioner of Construction
ch01.note: 张秋白. A real figure of this name existed in Nationalist politics; whether the historical man's career matches the office and the fate given here I have not been able to establish, and this book is not the sort of source that settles such questions. The nickname the text gives him — 张扒皮, "Zhang the Flayer," rendered below as the people of Anhui called him — is the traditional epithet for a rapacious official or landlord, the man who skins those under him.

ch01.anchor: the Ming emperor's tomb near at hand
ch01.note: 明孝陵, the Xiaoling mausoleum of the founding Ming emperor Zhu Yuanzhang, on the southern slope of Purple Mountain. Plum Blossom Hill (梅花山), where the killers lie up, is the tomb's forecourt hill — it holds the burial mound of Sun Quan, the third-century king of Wu. The author has chosen his ground: an ambush laid among six centuries of imperial dead.

ch01.anchor: war never tires of deception
ch01.note: 兵不厌诈, the proverbial condensation of Sun Tzu; and 虚而实之，实而虚之 — "empty where solid, solid where empty" — in the next breath is the Art of War's doctrine of feints, quoted by a gunman to justify storming a dinner party. Popular fiction likes its toughs classically read.

ch01.anchor: a high spirit screen carved with two characters — Great Felicity
ch01.note: The 影壁 or spirit screen is the free-standing wall just inside or before a traditional gate, blocking sight-lines (and, in folklore, straight-flying spirits). 鸿禧, "vast felicity," is a standard auspicious inscription; the author sets the word FELICITY over the door of the house where the wrong man is about to be shot, and I decline to believe that is an accident.

ch01.anchor: four Eight Immortals tables in a row
ch01.note: 八仙桌, the square table seating two a side, eight in all, named for the Eight Immortals of Daoist legend. The standard furniture of any formal Chinese dinner; kept literal here for its flavor.

ch01.anchor: An injustice has its author; a debt has its owner
ch01.note: 冤有头，债有主 — every wrong has a head, every debt a master: the classic announcement of Chinese underworld etiquette, spoken when armed men enter a room full of bystanders. It promises precision — we are here for one man — and it makes what actually happens at this banquet, three bullets into a man merely for delivering bad news, a self-indictment the author leaves entirely unremarked.

ch01.anchor: the familiar long horse-face
ch01.note: 马型长脸. Worth noting that the author has already shown us this face through Wang Yaqiao's binoculars in section 1, looking like "a man of letters." The horse-faced description here is the killers' file-photograph memory of the same man — the book is casual about focalization, and details shift with the describer.

prologue.note: 黄埔路, Huangpu Road, in Nanjing's northeastern quarter, took its name from the successor institutions of the Whampoa (Huangpu) Military Academy headquartered along it, and Chiang's famous residence-office there, the Qilu bungalow, was built only around 1929–31. Nothing places this scene's April 1927 summons at that address; the author is furnishing the story with the residence every later reader of Republican history knows. Uncorroborated for the date.

戴笠 Dai Li (1897–1946), original name Dai Chunfeng 戴春风, courtesy name Yunong 雨农, of Jiangshan, Zhejiang: later the chief of the Juntong military secret service and the most feared police figure of Nationalist China. 大特务, "the great special agent," is the stock villain epithet mainland popular history hangs on him. In April 1927 the real Dai Li was a thirty-year-old cadet of Whampoa's sixth class passing informal intelligence to Chiang; his formal intelligence career begins the following year. The book promotes him early, a chronology worth remembering through the whole prologue.

prologue.anchor: telephone call from the aides' office
prologue.note: 侍从室, the Attendants' Office, Chiang's personal secretariat, and 委座, "the Generalissimo" (literally the honored seat of the Military Affairs Commission chairmanship, rendered here by its English convention), are both institutions of the 1930s. In an April 1927 scene they are anachronisms, borrowed backward for atmosphere.

prologue.anchor: Blue Sky and White Sun flag
prologue.note: The party flag: white twelve-rayed sun on a blue field, with no red. The author hangs it over Chiang's desk and, at the end of the audience, seats him under the full national tricolor (the Blue Sky, White Sun, and Wholly Red Earth of chapter one's note); the two flags are different objects, and the book's usage keeps the distinction correctly.

校长, literally "Principal." Every Whampoa graduate addressed Chiang by his academy title for the rest of his life, answering for himself as 学生, "your student"; the pairing declares a bond of personal discipleship that outranked any formal chain of command. English convention for the academy post is Commandant, and this translation uses it wherever the address occurs.

prologue.anchor: Li Zongren, Feng Yuxiang, Yan Xishan
prologue.note: Li Zongren 李宗仁 (1891–1969), the Guangxi commander, was indeed a pillar of the new Nanjing regime. But Feng Yuxiang 冯玉祥 (1882–1948), the "Christian General," came to terms with Chiang only at the Xuzhou meeting in June 1927, and Yan Xishan 阎锡山 (1883–1960), the Shanxi "Model Governor," accepted a Nanjing command that same June. Neither attended the April 18 founding ceremony, so this photograph's rostrum is the author's tableau, not a document: contradicted by the record.

prologue.anchor: God damn his mother — the very man
prologue.note: 娘希匹 niang xipi, Chiang's notorious oath in his native Ningbo dialect, obscene and instantly recognizable; memoirists made it his verbal signature. English can carry the anger but not the dialect, which is half the characterization: every Chinese reader hears Chiang's own voice in these two syllables.

prologue.anchor: second only to the Green and Red Gangs
prologue.note: 青红帮, the Green Gang (Qingbang) and the older Red Gang (Hongbang) run together as one compound term for organized crime in Shanghai, as Chinese usage commonly does. The real power of the era was the Green Gang of Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng; ranking the Hatchet Gang "second only" to it is the author's flattery of his subject.

张啸林 Zhang Xiaolin (1877–1940), third of the "three great bosses" (三大亨) of the French Concession with Huang Jinrong and Du Yuesheng. He later collaborated with the Japanese occupation and was shot dead by his own bodyguard in 1940, a killing generally credited to Dai Li's service — one more thread binding this page's cast together. Corroborated.

prologue.anchor: eaten a bear's heart and a tiger's gall
prologue.note: The standard idiom is 吃了熊心豹子胆, "eaten a bear's heart and a leopard's gall"; the book prints a tiger 虎 in the leopard's place. Either way it names impossible, unnatural audacity: courage a man could only have swallowed whole from a beast.

prologue.anchor: the founding assembly of the National Government
prologue.note: The Nanjing National Government was proclaimed on April 18, 1927, at Dingjiaqiao, in the former Jiangsu provincial assembly hall, six days after Chiang's April 12 purge in Shanghai; Cai Yuanpei conferred the seals for the party and Hu Hanmin received them for the government. No account of the ceremony records a workers' delegate denouncing Chiang from the rostrum. Wang's documented standing in Shanghai's Anhui labor world makes the author's casting plausible; the scene itself is uncorroborated.

prologue.anchor: the Three Great Policies that every Nationalist is bound to keep
prologue.note: 联俄、联共、扶助农工: alliance with Russia, alliance with the Communists, succor for workers and peasants. The three had real standing in the reorganized party of 1924, but the packaged phrase "Three Great Policies" was consolidated by the Soviet advisers and the party's left wing, and Sun's actual deathbed testament does not contain it. Its attribution to Sun's dying charge has been fought over by Nationalist and Communist historiography ever since; the author gives Wang the Communist-canonical version, which is also what a left-leaning labor delegate of 1927 would in fact have said.

prologue.anchor: opened slaughter upon us — upon the workers
prologue.note: The April 12, 1927 coup: Chiang's forces and Green Gang auxiliaries broke the Communist-led General Labor Union in Shanghai, with hundreds killed in the days following. This, the one solidly documented event beneath the whole speech, had happened six days before the founding ceremony. Corroborated.

十人团. History knows a ten-man Liaison Group (联络组) formed under Dai Li in 1928 and later called the embryo of the whole Nationalist intelligence apparatus. The book moves it a year earlier, arms it, and hands it a murder brief; partly corroborated as an institution, contradicted in its chronology. Its members being brought "from Wuhan" is odd on its face — Wuhan was the seat of the rival left-Nationalist government Chiang was defying — and finds no echo in the record.

鸡鹅巷, "Chicken-and-Goose Lane," off Zhongshan North Road. The documented address is No. 53: from 1931 the courtyard at 鸡鹅巷53号 housed Dai Li's secret-police organs and his family both, and it remained the service's sanctum ("Office A") after the headquarters outgrew it. The book prints No. 54 here and No. 45 a few pages on — the scan is unambiguous in both places, so the inconsistency belongs to the author or his edition — and the address itself is another back-projection: in 1927 there was no such establishment for Dai Li to keep watch in.

The rescue story that follows is the book's engine for the whole Wang–Dai relationship, and no independent source records it. What the record does hold is that Dai Li in his drifting years attached himself to Wang Yaqiao, and Chinese reference accounts make Wang, Dai Li and the future general Hu Zongnan sworn brothers in that Shanghai period. Even the year sits oddly: in 1916 Dai was a nineteen-year-old in Zhejiang by most accounts, and his Shanghai drifting belongs to the early 1920s. Read it as a novelist's origin scene built over an attested tie.

十里洋场, "the ten-li foreign strip" (a li is about a third of a mile): the stock epithet for concession-era Shanghai, its glitter and its foreignness compressed into four characters. The phrase is worn smooth in Chinese; there is no equally worn English coin.

小瘪三, "little biesan": Shanghai slang for the destitute drifters of the concessions, a word with a pitying sneer built into it. Calling the future terror of Nationalist China a biesan is the sharpest class irony in the prologue, and untranslatable as a single word.

贺衷寒 He Zhongyan (1900–1972), of Whampoa's first class, later one of the leading figures of the Blue Shirt political-warfare apparatus — in the world of Chiang's political police he was senior to Dai Li, not his squadmate. His presence on this raid is the book's invention so far as the record shows; uncorroborated.
洪武街, a central Nanjing street named for the reign title of the Ming founder, whose capital Nanjing was. No independent record ties Wang Yaqiao's Nanjing lodging to it.

No April 1927 national warrant for Wang Yaqiao appears in the record; his documented notoriety and the great manhunts come later, with the attentats of 1931–1936 that fill the rest of this book. The overnight-celebrity flourish is the author's; uncorroborated.

ch02.anchor: March 1928, Hefei
ch02.note: The chapter's clock is the author's, not history's. The events it braids together are documented in 1929 and 1930: Chen Diaoyuan left the Anhui chairmanship and Fang Zhenwu received it in 1929; Fang was seized in September 1929; Wang Leping was assassinated in February 1930. Dating the whole braid "March 1928" compresses two years into one spring, and the notes below mark each strand's real date. Contradicted as chronology; the strands themselves are largely real.

ch02.anchor: the Tongmenghui dormitory compound
ch02.note: The Tongmenghui, the revolutionary league of 1905, dissolved into the Nationalist Party in 1912; a standing "provincial Tongmenghui" with offices and dormitories in 1928 Hefei is the author's furniture for the circle of 1911 veterans around Bo Wenwei. No such institution appears in the record.

ch02.anchor: Xiakou, a market town in Jiangshan county
ch02.note: Dai Li's documented birthplace is Baoan (保安), a village in the southern hills of Jiangshan county; Xiakou is a neighboring market town in the same valley. The book's placement is loose rather than wrong: Baoan lay under Xiakou's district in some period gazetteers. Jiangshan sits in Zhejiang's far southwest, and its dialect and poverty marked Dai Li's men: the service he later built promoted Jiangshan natives so heavily that colleagues joked about its "Jiangshan clique."

ch02.anchor: the Zhejiang warlord Zhou Fengqi
ch02.note: Zhou Fengqi (1879-1938), a Zhejiang division commander who crossed to the Nationalists in 1926-27; Dai Li's teenage service as an orderly in his ranks is standard in the biographies. Zhou's end completes a circle the author leaves undrawn: in March 1938, on his way to take office in the Japanese-sponsored regime at Nanjing, he was shot dead in the French Concession by gunmen of the very service his former orderly had built. Corroborated.

ch02.anchor: the old manner of Mao Sui
ch02.note: 毛遂自荐, "Mao Sui recommends himself": the Warring States retainer who, unasked, put himself forward to Lord Pingyuan of Zhao and proved indispensable. The four characters are the standard idiom for volunteering oneself; the beggar drafting his own letter of introduction by lamplight is playing a classical part, and a Chinese reader smiles at it.

ch02.anchor: bamboo-grove wars
ch02.note: 竹战, "bamboo warfare": a literary joke for mahjong, whose old tiles were bamboo-backed. The author's 竹林之战, "battle of the bamboo grove," dresses the gambling den in the clothes of the famous third-century Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove; the collision of hoodlums and high culture is the joke.

ch02.anchor: Eight Immortals table
ch02.note: 八仙桌: the big square table seating two a side, eight in all, named for the Eight Immortals of Daoist legend; the standard furniture of halls, teahouses and gambling rooms. Where one stands relative to such a table is a map of status, which is why Dai Chunfeng waits two hours beside it.

ch02.anchor: honor upheld and wealth scattered
ch02.note: 仗义疏财: the stock formula of praise for the outlaw-gentleman, worn smooth in Water Margin. To call a gang boss by it is to place him in the lineage of Liangshan heroes, exactly the self-image Wang Yaqiao cultivated.

ch02.anchor: smeared blood in covenant
ch02.note: 歃血为盟, the blood-smearing oath, sealed here by 换帖 (exchanging cards bearing each brother's birth-eight characters) and 磕头 (the kowtow) — the full ritual grammar of Republican-era sworn brotherhood, the 八拜之交 or "friendship of eight bows" the text later names. These bonds organized gangland, the army and politics alike; the book's whole tragedy runs on one of them.

ch02.anchor: Chiang Chung-cheng
ch02.note: 蒋中正, Chiang's formal adopted name ("central and upright"), the name on documents and monuments in the Nationalist world, given here in its Wade-Giles form as the register demands. Referring to oneself by full formal name — "me, Chiang Chung-cheng" — is the diction of a superior stating a fixed fact about the order of things.

ch02.anchor: his second elder brother from the founding of the Hatchet Gang
ch02.note: Here the book and the record part company. Wang Leping (王乐平, 1884-1930) was a Shandong Tongmenghui veteran and a leader of the Reorganizationists, the anti-Chiang opposition inside the Nationalist Party — after early 1929 its de facto chief in Shanghai. Nothing in the record makes him a founder or "second elder brother" of the Hatchet Gang. The photograph's original caption on this page, which calls him a core figure of the Reorganizationists' military campaign against Chiang, is in fact closer to the documented man than the prose beside it. His assassination is historical; see the note at its place below.

ch02.anchor: kill the wicked to succor the many
ch02.note: 杀恶济众. The creed matches the moral persona the popular tradition gives Wang Yaqiao — assassination as chivalric justice rather than crime — and his documented targets (militarists, collaborators, officials) gave the claim its purchase. It is self-presentation, not law: the same tradition records bodyguards and bystanders among his victims.

ch02.anchor: autocrat, that thief of the people
ch02.note: 独夫民贼. Two classical stones thrown as one: 独夫, the "lone man," is Mencius's word for a ruler whose crimes have stripped him of the Mandate (killing such a man, Mencius says, is not regicide), and 民贼, "thief of the people," is likewise Mencian. In Wang's mouth the phrase quietly claims a philosopher's license for assassination.

ch02.anchor: Fang Zhenwu arrived in Hefei to take up the provincial chairmanship
ch02.note: Fang Zhenwu (方振武, 1885-1941), Anhui-born Northern Expedition general, did succeed Chen Diaoyuan as chairman of Anhui — in May 1929, not 1928. His later life keeps faith with this chapter's casting: in 1933 he joined Feng Yuxiang's anti-Japanese army in Chahar against Nanjing's wishes, and in 1941 he was murdered — by most accounts at the hands of Chiang's agents. Corroborated, redated.

ch02.anchor: to link Fang Zhenwu, Shi Yousan and Bo Wenwei
ch02.note: Shi Yousan (石友三, 1891-1940) was the era's most notorious serial turncoat: he betrayed Feng Yuxiang three times, Chiang more than once, and finally treated with the Japanese, for which his own subordinate had him strangled and buried by the Yellow River in 1940. In December 1929 his artillery at Pukou shelled Nanjing itself in an abortive revolt — likely the seed of this chapter's "Shi Yousan's force was crushed." That Wang Yaqiao personally recruited him is the book's claim; uncorroborated.

ch02.anchor: the Independent Fourth Brigade at Changzhou
ch02.note: Neither an "Independent Fourth Brigade" at Changzhou nor its commander Peng Jianguo (彭建国) appears in the order-of-battle records or histories I could reach; the romanization is mine and the mutiny episode is uncorroborated. It reads as a composite of the small-garrison revolts that flickered along the Yangtze in 1929-30.

ch02.anchor: the Three Kingdoms set against one man
ch02.note: 三国一方: the plan is named for the storybook geometry of the Three Kingdoms, three powers boxing one hegemon. The allusion is load-bearing — it flatters the plotters with Zhuge Liang's strategic glamour, and it sets up the Jiang Gan joke a few pages on.

ch02.anchor: sixth class, in the cavalry section
ch02.note: Corroborated: Dai Li tested into the Whampoa Academy's sixth class, cavalry section — but in 1926, not on the heels of the book's 1925 departure from Shanghai, and he was a cadet still when the Northern Expedition began. The book consistently promotes his career a year or more ahead of the record.

ch02.anchor: Hardship Surpassing All
ch02.note: 艰苦卓绝, "hardship surpassing all": a stock four-character commendation. That Chiang brushed it for Dai Li personally is the book's ornament; I find no record of the inscription.

ch02.anchor: through the five northern provinces
ch02.note: Dai Li's runs into the warlord north as Chiang's private intelligence courier during the Northern Expedition are attested in outline in the scholarship; the itinerary given here (Tianjin, Beiping, Taiyuan, Zhengzhou, Xi'an) is the author's furnishing. Note the anachronism inside it: Beijing became "Beiping" only after the Expedition took it in mid-1928.

ch02.anchor: the party split between Nanjing and Wuhan
ch02.note: 宁汉分裂: from April to September 1927 the Nationalist movement had two rival seats, Chiang's new government at Nanjing and the left-Nationalist government at Wuhan under Wang Jingwei, with Tang Shengzhi's Hunan army as Wuhan's sword. Espionage between the two camps was a real trade; the next episode belongs to it.

ch02.anchor: the military secrets of Tang Shengzhi's army
ch02.note: Tang Shengzhi (唐生智, 1889-1970), the Hunanese general who was Wuhan's military mainstay and twice made war on Nanjing. Zhou Weilong (周伟龙) is real — a Whampoa man who became one of Dai Li's senior officers — and a Wuhan mission by Dai Li is attested in outline. The death sentence, the eve-of-execution interview and the jailbreak-by-persuasion are the popular tradition's embroidery; no documentary account confirms them. Attested in outline, dramatized in detail.

ch02.anchor: a secret telegram had come from Chiang Kai-shek personally
ch02.note: This is the one scene in the chapter the record confirms almost to the prop list. In September 1929 Fang Zhenwu was summoned to Nanjing by wire on the pretext of a military conference, seized on arrival, and put — in irons — into the Tangshan military prison; he was freed only after the Mukden Incident of September 1931 forced Chiang's retirement. The book keeps the telegram, the pretext and Tangshan, and moves the whole thing back a year and a half. Corroborated, redated.

ch02.anchor: Jiang Gan come to steal the letters
ch02.note: 蒋干盗书, Romance of the Three Kingdoms chapter 45: before Red Cliffs, Cao Cao sends the persuader Jiang Gan to his old schoolmate Zhou Yu, who feasts him on old friendship and plants a forged letter for him to steal, to fatal effect. "A Jiang Gan visit" is proverbial for the old friend who arrives wearing the enemy's errand. In Chinese the joke has a second blade the English cannot keep: Jiang Gan and Chiang Kai-shek share the surname 蒋.

ch02.anchor: well-water need not trouble river-water
ch02.note: 井水不犯河水: each to his own waters, a truce formula. Kept literal for its cool, proverbial finality.

ch02.anchor: walk without changing my name
ch02.note: 行不更名，坐不改姓: the outlaw's formula of self-declaration from Water Margin and its descendants — I am who I say, awake or asleep, and hide from no one. Another tessera of the greenwood self-image this book builds for Wang.

ch02.anchor: open the skylight and talk in the light
ch02.note: 打开天窗说亮话: "open the skylight and speak bright words" — no more talking in a dark room; the cards on the table. Kept literal because the image survives the crossing.

ch02.anchor: rising again in the eastern hills
ch02.note: 东山再起: the return of Xie An, the fourth-century statesman who left retirement in the Eastern Hills to save the Jin dynasty at the Fei River. The idiom is the standard hope of every defeated figure in Chinese; from a gang wife at a sickbed it borrows a very grand precedent.

ch02.anchor: wash the dust off his guest
ch02.note: 洗尘, "washing the dust": the welcome banquet owed a traveler at journey's end, classical hospitality. That Wang gives the ritual meal to the man he has just unmasked as his enemy's envoy is the scene's cold joke.

ch02.anchor: deep in the night of February 17
ch02.note: The assassination of Wang Leping is documented — and dated the night of February 18, 1930 (a killing after midnight on the 17th-18th may underlie the book's date), at his Reorganizationist office at 314 Route Cardinal Mercier in the French Concession, where gunmen burst in and shot him dead at forty-six; responsibility is generally laid to Chiang's agents. The book moves the scene to an ambush at his car near the Avenue Joffre lanes, hands the operation to Dai Li by name, and pulls it into its 1928 frame. The murder is corroborated; the staging and the date are the author's.

ch02.anchor: the Women's Northern Expedition Restoration Army
ch02.note: Women's military corps were real and celebrated in the 1911 revolution — Wuchang and Shanghai both raised them, with names built from 女子 (women's), 北伐 (northern expedition) and 光复 (restoration). The particular combined banner given here, and Cong Yunyu's command in it, I could not corroborate; the entire account of Wang's wife — original name, Wuhan rescue, remarriage of her surname — rests on the book and the popular tradition behind it. Her renaming runs the same track as her husband's courtesy name: 亚英 "second-hero" beside his 亚樵.

ch02.anchor: rather live on his feet than die on his knees
ch02.note: So the scan reads, unambiguously: 宁可站着生，也不跪着死 — "rather live standing than die kneeling." The book's own table of contents, at chapter four, prints the maxim the standard way around ("rather die standing than never live kneeling" — 宁可站着死，绝不跪着生). Either the author varied it or the compositor slipped; I translate what this page prints and flag the variance.

ch02.anchor: His name was Zhao Tieqiao
ch02.note: Zhao Tieqiao (赵铁桥, 1886-1930): a Tongmenghui veteran of the Sichuan revolution who became a Chiang loyalist, and from 1929 supervisor (总办) of the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company, where his housecleaning made rich enemies. On July 24, 1930 he was shot dead at the company's gate on the Shanghai Bund — a killing the whole tradition credits to Wang Yaqiao's men; accounts even name Wang Ganting and Niu Anru, familiar from chapter one, among the shooters. That he was the informer who broke Wang's 1929-30 anti-Chiang organizing is the popular tradition's motive, and the book's; the rival documented motive is the struggle for the shipping company itself. Chapter three is his story; both versions are weighed there.
